target_skill: Identify and name the epidemiologic concept of public health surveillance from a plain-language description.
novel_context: A county health department sets up a system where school nurses report the number of students with flu-like symptoms each week. Staff regularly organize and review these reports to decide if they need to start vaccination campaigns or send health alerts.
fixed_givens: Health staff are collecting health-related data from schools on a regular, repeating schedule.
They organize (analyze) and review the information that comes in.
They use what they learn from the data to decide on public health actions (like vaccination campaigns or alerts).
The question asks for the epidemiologic term for this overall activity.

nodes.label: Data about student flu-like illness are collected from schools on a routine, ongoing basis.
The health department organizes and reviews (analyzes and interprets) these data.
The information is used to guide decisions about prevention and control actions.
Name the epidemiologic term for this organized, ongoing health data system.
Answer must be a standard basic-epidemiology term appropriate for Division B (grades 6–9).
Confusing the overall system (surveillance) with a specific study design (e.g., cohort or case-control study).

distractor_mechanisms: Answering with a specific study design name (e.g., 'case-control study', 'cohort study') instead of the broader system-level term.
Answering with 'screening' or 'diagnosis', focusing on individual patients rather than population-level data systems.
Answering with a general phrase like 'data collection' or 'monitoring' without recognizing the established epidemiology term.

target_skill: Identify and name key person, place, and time elements used to describe who is included in an outbreak.
novel_context: A cluster of stomach illness among students after a school event in a fictional town.
fixed_givens: In the town of Riverbend, several students from Oak Hill Middle School go to the emergency room with severe vomiting and diarrhea over a few days.
The local health department notices that the number of these stomach illness cases from Oak Hill Middle School is much higher than they usually see in one week.
Officials suspect these illnesses might be part of the same outbreak and want to write a clear description of which cases will be counted in the investigation.
They know they should describe cases using the standard outbreak description of who is affected, where they were exposed or became sick, and when they became sick.

Question prompt to students: When defining which illnesses belong in this suspected outbreak, besides the type of symptoms, list any TWO of the three basic descriptive features (from “person, place, and time”) that investigators should clearly state for the outbreak cases.

nodes.label: Health officials suspect a group of stomach illness cases among students at one middle school are part of the same outbreak.
They want to describe which illnesses will be counted in the outbreak using basic descriptive epidemiology.
Standard outbreak descriptions commonly use person, place, and time to define which cases belong to an outbreak.
Identify that two of the three aspects—person (who), place (where), time (when)—must be clearly described for outbreak cases.

verification.expected_answer: Any two of the following: person (who is affected, such as students at Oak Hill Middle School), place (where they were exposed or became sick, such as a specific school or town), and time (when they became sick, such as a certain week or date range).

distractor_mechanisms: Listing the cause of illness (e.g., a specific food or germ) instead of basic descriptive features.
Listing specific symptoms (e.g., vomiting, diarrhea) even though the question asks for person, place, and time.
Listing laboratory tests or treatments (e.g., stool cultures, medications) instead of descriptive criteria.

target_skill: Explain why an observational study (such as a case-control study) showing a strong association does not, by itself, prove that an exposure is the definite cause or source of an outbreak.
novel_context: Students and families from several schools attended an indoor community sports tournament. Within two days, many people developed sudden vomiting and diarrhea. Disease detectives conducted a case-control study and found that people who drank smoothies from Vendor A were much more likely to be ill than those who did not. No germs have yet been found in leftover smoothies from Vendor A.
fixed_givens: An outbreak of vomiting and diarrhea occurred after an indoor community sports tournament.
Investigators did a case-control study comparing ill (cases) and not ill (controls) attendees.
People who drank smoothies from Vendor A were much more likely to be ill than people who did not drink Vendor A smoothies.
No infectious agent has yet been detected in leftover smoothies from Vendor A.
Question prompt: At this point in the investigation, can Vendor A smoothies be said to be the definite source of the outbreak? Answer "Yes" or "No" and briefly justify your answer.

nodes.label: Case-control study shows a strong association between Vendor A smoothies and illness.
No infectious agent has been found in leftover smoothies from Vendor A yet.
Observational studies (like case-control) can show associations but do not, by themselves, prove causation.
Confirming a definite source usually requires multiple lines of evidence, such as laboratory confirmation plus consistent epidemiologic findings.
Decide whether Vendor A smoothies can already be called the definite source of the outbreak and justify the answer.
Difficulty 1/5: reasoning should stay at the level of basic association vs causation and awareness of the limits of study design.

edges.label: Strong association suggests Vendor A smoothies are a likely source but is not final proof.
Lack of lab confirmation means the source is not yet definitively proven.
Explains why a case-control study alone cannot prove Vendor A smoothies are the definite source.
Clarifies that more evidence is normally needed for a definite conclusion.
Guides the level of explanation expected in the justification.

verification.expected_answer: No. A case-control study only shows an association; without laboratory confirmation or additional supporting evidence, Vendor A smoothies cannot yet be called the definite source of the outbreak.

distractor_mechanisms: Assuming any strong association in an observational study automatically proves causation and identifies the definite source.
Believing that laboratory confirmation is never needed once a statistical association is found.
Misunderstanding the purpose of a case-control study and thinking it is an experimental (intervention) study that can by itself prove cause and effect.

target_skill: Use a simple table of odds ratios from a case-control study to identify which exposure is most strongly associated with illness.
novel_context: Students at a week-long middle school science camp reported sudden stomach illness. Investigators conducted a case-control study of foods served at one camp lunch and calculated odds ratios for each food item.
fixed_givens: A case-control study was done among campers who attended a specific lunch.
Ill campers were cases; campers who ate lunch but did not become ill were controls.
Investigators calculated odds ratios (OR) for several foods served at that lunch.
Odds ratios greater than 1 suggest a positive association between eating that food and becoming ill; higher odds ratios mean a stronger association.

The following odds ratios were estimated for five food items:

Food item | Odds ratio (OR)
--------- | ---------------
Fruit salad | 1.4
Grilled fish | 3.2
Whole-grain bread | 0.9
Tomato soup | 1.1
Cooked carrots | 2.0
Question: Based on these odds ratios, which food item is most likely linked to the outbreak of illness?

nodes.label: Table lists odds ratios for five specific food items: fruit salad (1.4), grilled fish (3.2), whole-grain bread (0.9), tomato soup (1.1), cooked carrots (2.0).
Odds ratios greater than 1 indicate a positive association between eating the food and becoming ill; larger odds ratios indicate a stronger association.
Identify which single food item has the strongest association with illness based on the odds ratios.
Compare all odds ratios to find the largest value: 3.2 (grilled fish) is the highest among the listed foods.
Name grilled fish as the food item most likely linked to the outbreak.

verification.calculation: Identify the largest odds ratio in the table (3.2 for grilled fish), then select grilled fish as the item most likely linked to illness.

distractor_mechanisms: Student selects the food with odds ratio closest to 1 instead of the largest value, misunderstanding that higher OR means stronger association.
Student chooses a food with OR slightly above 1 (e.g., fruit salad at 1.4) because it seems more common or familiar, ignoring the numerical comparison.
Student incorrectly thinks OR < 1 (whole-grain bread, 0.9) means higher risk and selects it, reversing the interpretation of odds ratios.

target_skill: Use data from a simple graph to calculate and compare risk (cumulative incidence) between two groups by computing a risk ratio.
novel_context: Workers at a small electronics assembly plant report a new cough-and-fever illness during one month. A health team creates a bar graph showing, for each of two departments, how many workers became sick out of the total number of workers in that department.
fixed_givens: A bar graph compares two departments at the same workplace during the same one-month period.
For Department X, the bar is labeled: 40 workers sick out of 200 total workers.
For Department Y, the bar is labeled: 10 workers sick out of 200 total workers.
Students are told to treat these as cumulative risks over that month (number sick / total workers in each department).
Question prompt: "Using the information from the graph, calculate the risk ratio for the illness in Department X compared to Department Y. Show the value as a number (no units)."

nodes.label: Department X: 40 sick out of 200 workers in one month.
Department Y: 10 sick out of 200 workers in the same month.
Risk is defined here as number sick divided by total workers in that department over the month.
Calculate risk in Department X.
Calculate risk in Department Y.
Calculate risk ratio (RR) of illness in Department X compared to Department Y.

verification.calculation: Risk in Department X = 40/200 = 0.20. Risk in Department Y = 10/200 = 0.05. Risk ratio (X compared to Y) = 0.20 / 0.05 = 4.0.

distractor_mechanisms: Compute risk difference instead of risk ratio (0.20 - 0.05 = 0.15).
Invert the risk ratio by dividing Y risk by X risk (0.05 / 0.20 = 0.25).
Use raw counts instead of risks and calculate 40 / 10 = 4 without recognizing that equal denominators happen to cancel here, leading to correct value but for the wrong reasoning.

target_skill: Use a bar graph of odds ratios from a case-control study to identify which exposure is most strongly associated with illness.
novel_context: Middle school students attend an after-school robotics club party where several snack foods are served. Many students later develop a stomach illness, and investigators conduct a case-control study and graph the odds ratios for each snack food.
fixed_givens: Scenario: Students from a middle school robotics club hold an indoor celebration after a competition. At the party, several different snack foods are served. The next day, a number of students report nausea and vomiting.

Study design: Disease detectives perform a case-control study comparing students who became ill with those who stayed well. They calculate odds ratios (ORs) for several snack foods served at the party.

Graph description: A bar graph titled 'Odds Ratios for Snack Foods and Illness after Robotics Party' is provided. The x-axis lists snack foods, and the y-axis shows odds ratio (OR). Each bar is clearly labeled with its OR value.
Bar 1: Pretzel mix — OR = 0.7
Bar 2: Fruit salad cups — OR = 1.4
Bar 3: Mini veggie sandwiches — OR = 1.6
Bar 4: String cheese sticks — OR = 3.2
Bar 5: Lemon cookies — OR = 1.1
Assumption: All odds ratios are calculated correctly, and higher odds ratios (greater than 1) suggest a stronger association between that food and illness.
Question to student: Based on the odds ratios shown in the bar graph, which single snack food is most likely associated with the outbreak of stomach illness?

nodes.label: A bar graph shows odds ratios for five snack foods: pretzel mix (0.7), fruit salad cups (1.4), mini veggie sandwiches (1.6), string cheese sticks (3.2), lemon cookies (1.1).
Higher odds ratios greater than 1 indicate a stronger association between that food and illness.
Identify which snack food is most likely associated with the outbreak of stomach illness.
Among foods with OR > 1, the largest odds ratio is 3.2 for string cheese sticks.
Choosing a food with OR close to 1 (weak association), such as lemon cookies (1.1), instead of the highest OR.
Incorrectly choosing pretzel mix (OR < 1), which suggests a protective or negative association, not the likely source.

verification.expected_answer: String cheese sticks are most likely associated with the outbreak (they have the highest odds ratio, 3.2).

distractor_mechanisms: Selecting the food with odds ratio closest to 1.0 instead of the largest odds ratio above 1.0.
Misinterpreting an odds ratio less than 1 (pretzel mix, OR = 0.7) as indicating higher risk rather than lower risk.
Assuming the food that seems less healthy (e.g., lemon cookies) must be the source regardless of the data shown in the graph.

target_skill: Use a simple epidemic curve and exposure information to infer the most likely primary mode of transmission for an outbreak.
novel_context: A week-long city youth theater workshop where participants spend most of each day rehearsing indoors, with a bar graph showing new cases of a cough-and-fever illness by day of onset.
fixed_givens: A city arts council runs a 7-day indoor youth theater workshop for students ages 11–14.
All 60 participants eat the same catered lunch together only on Day 1; no shared meals are served on later days.
A bar graph (epidemic curve) shows the number of new workshop participants who develop cough and fever each day from Day 2 through Day 8.
On the graph, few cases appear on Day 2–3, more cases appear on Day 4–5, and the numbers then decrease on Day 6–8, forming several rising and falling bars rather than a single sharp spike.
Illness is reported almost entirely among workshop participants, who rehearse closely together indoors, with very little illness reported among staff family members at home.
Local health officials report no increase in mosquito populations or other insect-borne diseases in the city during this period.
Question prompt: Based only on the information provided (including the shape of the bar graph), what is the most likely main way this illness is spreading among workshop participants?

nodes.label: The epidemic curve shows a gradual rise in new cases over several days, then a fall, suggesting a propagated (person-to-person) pattern rather than a single sharp spike.
All participants shared the same catered lunch only on Day 1, but illness onsets are spread over many days, not clustered tightly after the meal.
Cases are mainly among people who spend hours together indoors at the workshop, and there is no evidence of increased mosquito activity or other insect-borne disease in the area.
Infer that the most likely main mode of transmission is person-to-person spread through respiratory droplets (e.g., coughing and close contact).
Assume the shared Day 1 meal is the primary source and conclude the illness is mainly foodborne, ignoring the multi-day propagated pattern.

verification.expected_answer: Person-to-person transmission through respiratory droplets (spread by coughing and close contact).

distractor_mechanisms: Focusing only on the shared Day 1 meal and assuming a foodborne common-source outbreak without considering the multi-day shape of the epidemic curve.
Ignoring the indoor close-contact setting and instead attributing the outbreak to mosquito-borne or other vector-borne transmission despite no supporting evidence.
Confusing the gradual rise-and-fall epidemic pattern with a single-exposure spike and therefore misclassifying the mode of transmission.

target_skill: Use basic properties of different pathogen groups (living vs. non-living, ability to reproduce in food vs. only in host cells) to identify which group cannot multiply in food before it is eaten.
novel_context: A county health department reviews one year of school cafeteria illness investigations. They create a bar graph showing the number of confirmed outbreaks linked to four agent categories: bacteria, viruses, parasites, and chemical toxins. A note under the graph reminds students that some agents can actually multiply in food before it is served, while others only contaminate the food without increasing in number.
fixed_givens: A bar graph is provided with four bars labeled: Bacteria, Viruses, Parasites, Chemical toxins.
The height of each bar shows the number of confirmed school cafeteria outbreaks in the past year caused by that agent type.

A caption states: 'Some agent types can grow and reproduce in food under the right conditions before people eat it. Other agent types can be present in food but do not increase their numbers there; they only multiply after entering host cells or do not reproduce at all.'

The question stem: 'Using the bar graph and your knowledge of pathogen groups, name the major group of infectious agents that cannot increase in number while in the food itself, but can still cause illness when the contaminated food is eaten.'

nodes.label: Graph shows outbreaks categorized by agent group: bacteria, viruses, parasites, chemical toxins.
Caption explains some agents can reproduce in food; others only contaminate food without multiplying there.
Viruses are non-living infectious agents that require living host cells to replicate; they do not multiply in food outside host cells.
Bacteria and some parasites are living organisms that can reproduce in or on food under suitable conditions.
Chemical toxins are not infectious agents and do not reproduce; they are not classified as a pathogen group like bacteria, viruses, or parasites.
Identify the major pathogen group that cannot increase in number in food but can still cause illness when contaminated food is eaten.
Misinterpret the graph and choose the bar with the fewest outbreaks instead of using biological properties of each agent group.

distractor_mechanisms: Choosing 'bacteria' because many students associate foodborne illness mainly with bacterial contamination, ignoring that bacteria can grow in food.
Choosing 'chemical toxins' by focusing on the fact that they do not reproduce, without recognizing that they are not part of the main pathogen groups being compared (bacteria, viruses, parasites).

Picking the category with the smallest bar on the graph under the mistaken assumption that fewer outbreaks mean the agent is less able to grow in food, instead of using biological reasoning about replication requirements.

target_skill: Use a simple comparison graph of illness between two exposure groups to suggest a practical prevention measure that targets the higher-risk behavior.
novel_context: A city library hosts a weekend youth science fair with interactive stations and shared snacks. After the event, many children report a brief vomiting and diarrhea illness. Investigators create a bar graph showing the percentage of children who became ill among (1) those who used a popular shared touchscreen station and then immediately ate snacks without cleaning their hands, and (2) those who cleaned their hands at a nearby hand-cleaning station before eating.
fixed_givens: Fictional setting: A weekend youth science fair at a city library with several hands-on exhibit stations and a shared snack table (vegetable sticks and dip).
Several children develop a short-lasting vomiting and diarrhea illness within 1–2 days after the event.

Investigators interview children and determine whether they: (a) used a busy shared touchscreen station and then ate snacks right away without cleaning their hands, or (b) used the touchscreen but cleaned their hands at the hand-cleaning station before eating.
A bar graph is provided with two bars, each labeled with an attack rate (risk) of illness among children who used the touchscreen station:
Group 1 ("Touched screen, ate snacks right away, no hand cleaning"): 40% of these children became ill.
Group 2 ("Touched screen, then cleaned hands before eating"): 10% of these children became ill.
Assume the illness is spread mainly by germs on hands that can contaminate food when people eat with their fingers.

Prompt to competitors: "Using the information in the bar graph and the description above, give ONE specific action the library staff could take before or during the next science fair to help prevent a similar outbreak of stomach illness."

Answers should be focused on changing behaviors or conditions related to hand cleanliness before eating the shared snacks (for example, policies, supplies, or staff instructions), not on medical treatment after people are already sick.

nodes.label: Children who touched the shared touchscreen and then ate snacks without cleaning their hands had a 40% illness rate.
Children who touched the same touchscreen but cleaned their hands before eating had a 10% illness rate.
The illness is mainly spread by germs on hands that can get onto food when eating with fingers.
Not cleaning hands before eating after using the touchscreen is associated with a higher risk of illness than cleaning hands.
Reducing the number of children who eat without cleaning their hands after using the touchscreen should lower the number of illnesses.

A specific prevention action is proposed that increases or enforces hand cleaning before eating (e.g., requiring or strongly encouraging handwashing/hand sanitizer use before visiting the snack table, adding clearly marked hand-cleaning stations right by the snacks, or having staff remind or supervise children to clean hands before taking food).
Suggesting only treatment for sick children (e.g., giving medicine) without changing behaviors before eating does not address prevention of future cases.

Suggesting a change that does not affect hand contamination or eating behavior (e.g., "move the touchscreen to another room" without any hand-cleaning intervention) does not directly target the higher-risk behavior shown in the graph.

verification.expected_answer: Require or clearly enforce that children clean their hands (for example, washing with soap and water or using hand sanitizer at a station placed right next to the snack table) after using the touchscreen and before eating the shared snacks.
verification.calculation: Conceptual prevention question based on comparing two attack rates; no numeric calculation is required.

distractor_mechanisms: Focusing on treatment instead of prevention (e.g., suggesting medicine or staying home when sick, which does not change the exposure that led to illness at the event).
Proposing a very general answer like "be cleaner" without specifying an actionable step linked to hand cleaning before eating.

Suggesting changes that do not address hand-to-food transmission (e.g., rearranging exhibits, changing snack types without reducing hand contamination, or limiting time at the touchscreen without any hand-cleaning requirement).

target_skill: Use a time-trend graph of reported cases along with information about a surveillance system change to judge whether a sudden increase likely reflects a real rise in disease or a change in reporting.
novel_context: A city health department monitors sudden breathing problems among middle school students using emergency department (ED) reports. In May, they switch from a paper-based system (hospitals mail weekly tallies) to an automatic electronic reporting system that sends daily case counts.
fixed_givens: A line graph titled 'Reported ED Visits for Sudden Breathing Problems Among Middle School Students, City Z, January–December' with months on the x-axis (Jan–Dec) and number of reported visits on the y-axis.
For January–April, reported visits are stable at about 10–14 visits per month with small up-and-down variation.
In May, an arrow on the graph marks 'Start of new electronic ED reporting system'.
Reported visits jump from 12 in April to 24 in May, then stay between 22–26 visits per month from June through December without a steady upward or downward trend.
No major weather event, wildfire, or new industrial source of air pollution is reported during the year.
Hospitals report that the way they diagnose and treat breathing problems has not changed during the year.
Health officials want to know if the jump in reported visits after May more likely represents a true increase in breathing problems or a change caused by the new surveillance system.
prompt: Based on the pattern shown in the graph and the information provided, is the sharp increase in reported ED visits for sudden breathing problems after May more likely due mainly to (a) a real rise in breathing problems among students or (b) the change in the surveillance system? Briefly state which one you think is more likely and give one piece of evidence from the graph or description to support your answer.

nodes.label: From January–April, reported ED visits stay roughly stable at 10–14 per month.
In May, a new electronic ED reporting system starts (arrow on graph).
Reported visits jump from 12 in April to 24 in May, right when the electronic system begins.
From June–December, reported visits remain fairly stable at 22–26 per month (no continuing upward trend).
No big environmental change (like wildfires or new pollution sources) and no change in clinical diagnosis are reported during the year.
Decide whether the sharp increase in reported visits after May is more likely due mainly to a real increase in disease or to the surveillance system change.

If a sudden, step-like change in case counts occurs exactly when the surveillance method changes, and levels then stay at a new plateau, this often indicates improved detection/reporting rather than a true sudden doubling of disease risk.

True increases in disease due to environmental or exposure changes often show additional supporting evidence (known exposure events) or a continuing trend, not just a one-time step change tied to a reporting change.
Answer must be supported by at least one piece of evidence from the graph or description (not just a guess).

verification.expected_answer: Most of the increase is more likely due to the surveillance system change (the new electronic reporting), not a sudden real doubling of breathing problems. Evidence: the sharp step up in reported visits happens exactly when the new reporting system starts and then stays at a new, steady level for the rest of the year, without a continuing upward trend or known environmental change.
distractor_mechanisms: Assuming any increase on a graph must represent a real increase in disease and ignoring the timing of the surveillance system change.
Focusing on the higher numbers after May without noticing that they form a flat plateau rather than a continuing upward trend.
Attributing the increase to an unspecified environmental cause (like 'bad air') even though the problem states there were no major environmental changes.
